````markdown
# Unity: The Power of Shared Identity

Unity is the seventh and newest principle in Cialdini's framework, added in the expanded edition of "Influence." It goes beyond liking (I'm similar to this person) to identity (this person IS one of us). Unity is about shared identity, tribal belonging, and the deep human need to be part of something larger than oneself.

This reference covers the distinction between unity and liking, sources of tribal identity, building community identity in products, the language of unity, identity marketing, co-creation as a unity driver, and detailed real-world examples.

## Unity vs. Liking: The Critical Distinction

This distinction is essential to applying unity correctly:

| Dimension | Liking | Unity |
|-----------|--------|-------|
| **Core feeling** | "This person is similar to me" | "This person IS me / one of us" |
| **Relationship** | Affinity, friendliness | Identity, belonging |
| **Basis** | Shared traits, attractiveness | Shared identity, tribe membership |
| **Strength** | Moderate influence | Very strong influence |
| **Reversibility** | Easy to stop liking | Hard to leave an identity |
| **Behavioral effect** | More likely to comply | Willing to sacrifice |
| **Example** | "I like this brand" | "I AM a [brand community member]" |

**The test**: Liking means you think positively about something. Unity means you define yourself partly through your connection to it. A person who likes Apple products is experiencing liking. A person who says "I'm an Apple person" is experiencing unity.

## Sources of Tribal Identity

### 1. Kinship and Family

**Mechanism**: The strongest unity comes from real or perceived family bonds. Even invoking family language creates stronger bonds.

| Application | Example | Why It Works |
|-------------|---------|-------------|
| Family language | "Welcome to the family" | Triggers deepest belonging instincts |
| Origin stories | "We started in a garage, like you" | Shared humble beginnings |
| Generational identity | "Built by millennials, for millennials" | Age cohort as family |
| Chosen family | "Your work family" | Extends kinship to non-relatives |

### 2. Place and Origin

**Mechanism**: Where we come from is core to identity. Geography creates automatic unity with others from the same place.

| Application | Example | Why It Works |
|-------------|---------|-------------|
| Local identity | "Made in Brooklyn" | Pride in place of origin |
| National identity | "An American company" | Patriotic association |
| Remote identity | "For the distributed team" | Location as shared experience |
| Diaspora | "For Nigerians abroad" | Shared experience of displacement |

### 3. Shared Experience

**Mechanism**: Going through the same experiences, especially difficult ones, creates powerful bonds. Shared struggle is one of the strongest unity builders.

| Application | Example | Why It Works |
|-------------|---------|-------------|
| Shared pain | "We've all struggled with bad CRMs" | Common enemy unites |
| Shared journey | "Fellow bootstrappers" | Shared path creates kinship |
| Shared achievement | "For people who ship" | Accomplished identity group |
| Shared transition | "New parents figuring it out together" | Vulnerable shared experience |

### 4. Shared Values and Beliefs

**Mechanism**: Deep values and beliefs form the core of identity. People who share your fundamental worldview feel like "us."

| Application | Example | Why It Works |
|-------------|---------|-------------|
| Mission alignment | "For people who believe work should be flexible" | Shared ideology |
| Ethical stance | "Privacy-first. Always." | Values as identity marker |
| Worldview | "For the optimistic builders" | Shared lens on the world |
| Opposition to status quo | "For those who refuse to settle" | Shared enemy or frustration |

### 5. Co-creation and Shared Action

**Mechanism**: Acting together, especially creating something together, generates unity. This is why sports teams, band members, and co-founders have such strong bonds.

| Application | Example | Why It Works |
|-------------|---------|-------------|
| Open source | "Built by the community, for the community" | Shared ownership |
| User feedback | "You asked for it, we built it" | Collaborative creation |
| Beta testing | "Help us shape the product" | Investment in outcome |
| Content creation | "Our community writes the playbook" | Collective knowledge |

## Building Community Identity in Products

### The Identity Architecture Framework

Build product identity through four layers:

**Layer 1: Name and Language**

| Element | Generic (Weak Unity) | Identity-Driven (Strong Unity) |
|---------|---------------------|-------------------------------|
| Community name | "Users", "Customers" | "Makers", "Builders", "Pilots" |
| Greeting | "Hello, user" | "Welcome back, maker" |
| Actions | "Submit", "Create" | "Ship", "Launch", "Build" |
| Achievements | "Level 2 user" | "Founding Builder" |

**Layer 2: Rituals and Traditions**

| Ritual | Example | Unity Effect |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| Daily standup | Product Hunt daily launch ritual | Shared daily experience |
| Weekly event | "Build in Public" weekly share | Recurring community moment |
| Annual celebration | GitHub Universe, Figma Config | Pilgrimage that reinforces belonging |
| Onboarding ritual | "Your first ship" achievement | Initiation into the tribe |
| Milestone celebration | "100th customer" community shoutout | Shared success moments |

**Layer 3: Symbols and Artifacts**

| Symbol | Example | Unity Effect |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| Logo/badge | GitHub contributor badge | Visible identity marker |
| Merchandise | Branded swag, stickers | Physical identity signal |
| Visual language | Consistent illustration style | Shared aesthetic identity |
| Inside jokes | Community memes, references | Exclusive shared knowledge |
| Leaderboards | Contribution rankings | Status within the tribe |

**Layer 4: Shared Enemies and Differentiation**

| Approach | Example | Unity Effect |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| Common frustration | "Tired of bloated software?" | United against a shared problem |
| Alternative identity | "We're not enterprise. We're indie." | Self-definition by contrast |
| Mission opposition | "Fight for user privacy" | United against a common threat |
| Quality standard | "We don't do mediocre" | Shared standard of excellence |

## The Language of Unity

### "We" vs. "You" Language

The words you choose signal whether the user is an outsider or an insider.

| Context | "You" Language (Liking) | "We" Language (Unity) |
|---------|------------------------|----------------------|
| **Feature announcement** | "You can now use..." | "We just shipped..." |
| **Problem framing** | "Your challenge is..." | "We all know the pain of..." |
| **Success** | "You achieved great results" | "We hit a new milestone together" |
| **Roadmap** | "Here's what's coming for you" | "Here's what we're building next" |
| **Support** | "How can I help you?" | "Let's figure this out together" |

### Identity Language Patterns

| Pattern | Example | Unity Mechanism |
|---------|---------|----------------|
| **"For [identity]"** | "For indie hackers" | Explicit identity inclusion |
| **"We are [identity]"** | "We are builders" | Shared identity declaration |
| **"[Identity] don't..."** | "Makers don't wait for permission" | Identity-based behavior norms |
| **"Join [identity]"** | "Join the movement" | Invitation into the tribe |
| **"[Identity] know that..."** | "Founders know that speed matters" | Insider knowledge signal |

### Inclusive vs. Exclusive Language

| Inclusive Unity | Exclusive Unity |
|----------------|----------------|
| "Everyone who cares about [value]" | "For the top 1% of [role]" |
| "Join a growing community of..." | "Apply to join. Not everyone gets in." |
| "We welcome all builders" | "Only serious practitioners" |

Both approaches work. Inclusive unity builds larger communities. Exclusive unity builds tighter, more committed ones. Choose based on your product strategy.

## Identity Marketing Strategies

### The Identity Marketing Formula

1. **Name the tribe**: Give your audience an identity label
2. **Define the worldview**: What does this tribe believe?
3. **Identify the enemy**: What does this tribe stand against?
4. **Create rituals**: What does this tribe do regularly?
5. **Provide symbols**: How does this tribe signal membership?

### Identity Marketing by Audience

| Audience | Identity Label | Worldview | Enemy |
|----------|---------------|-----------|-------|
| Startup founders | "Builders" | "Ship fast, learn fast" | Bureaucracy, slow corporations |
| Designers | "Creatives" | "Design matters" | Ugly, thoughtless products |
| Developers | "Makers" | "Code should be clean" | Technical debt, bloatware |
| Marketers | "Growth minds" | "Data drives decisions" | Vanity metrics, guesswork |
| Remote workers | "Digital nomads" | "Work from anywhere" | 9-to-5 office culture |

## Co-Creation as a Unity Driver

### Why Co-Creation Works

When users help build the product, they become part of its identity. Their fingerprints are on it. This creates a sense of ownership and belonging that no amount of marketing can replicate.

### Co-Creation Mechanisms

| Mechanism | Example | Unity Strength |
|-----------|---------|---------------|
| **Feature voting** | Public roadmap with user votes | Moderate (low effort) |
| **Beta testing** | Early access in exchange for feedback | Strong (active participation) |
| **Template sharing** | Users create and share templates | Very strong (creative investment) |
| **Content creation** | User-generated tutorials, guides | Very strong (knowledge sharing) |
| **Open source** | Community contributes code | Strongest (deep technical investment) |
| **Advisory board** | Customer advisory council | Very strong (strategic partnership) |

### Co-Creation Best Practices

1. **Acknowledge contributions publicly**: Name the users who helped shape features
2. **Close the loop**: When you build something users asked for, tell them it was their idea
3. **Give ownership**: Let users claim authorship of their contributions
4. **Create contributor tiers**: Recognize different levels of contribution
5. **Make co-creation visible**: Show the community what's being built together

## Real-World Examples

### Apple

**Unity mechanism**: Apple users don't just like Apple products; they identify as "Apple people."

| Element | Implementation | Unity Effect |
|---------|---------------|-------------|
| "Think Different" | Values-based identity positioning | "We are the creative ones" |
| Apple ecosystem | Products that work together exclusively | "Our world is different" |
| Apple Store experience | Community events, workshops | Shared gathering place |
| Product launches | Communal anticipation and excitement | Shared ritual |
| Design language | Consistent, recognizable aesthetic | Visual identity marker |

### CrossFit

**Unity mechanism**: CrossFit is not just a workout; it is an identity and a community.

| Element | Implementation | Unity Effect |
|---------|---------------|-------------|
| "Box" (not gym) | Unique language | Insider vocabulary |
| WOD (Workout of the Day) | Shared daily ritual | Everyone does the same thing |
| CrossFit Games | Aspirational shared event | Community pilgrimage |
| Shared suffering | Intense group workouts | Bonding through struggle |
| Lifestyle identity | "I do CrossFit" as self-description | Identity, not just activity |

### Notion

**Unity mechanism**: Notion built a community of "Notion ambassadors" who evangelize and co-create.

| Element | Implementation | Unity Effect |
|---------|---------------|-------------|
| Template gallery | User-created templates shared publicly | Co-creation and ownership |
| Ambassador program | Community leaders with special access | Tiered identity within tribe |
| Community forums | Active spaces for sharing workflows | Shared knowledge and rituals |
| "Made with Notion" | Badge for websites and pages | Visible identity signal |
| Flexible product | Users build unique systems | Personal investment and ownership |

### Indie Hackers

**Unity mechanism**: Indie Hackers created a tribe around the identity of building profitable internet businesses independently.

| Element | Implementation | Unity Effect |
|---------|---------------|-------------|
| Identity label | "Indie hacker" as self-description | Named tribe |
| Shared values | Profitability over fundraising | Worldview differentiation |
| Build in public | Transparent revenue sharing | Shared vulnerability and trust |
| Community forum | Active discussion of indie business | Daily tribal gathering |
| Podcast interviews | Members' stories featured | Hero stories reinforce identity |

## Unity Anti-Patterns

### What to Avoid

| Anti-Pattern | Problem | Better Approach |
|-------------|---------|----------------|
| **Toxic tribalism** | "We're better than them" messaging | Define identity positively, not antagonistically |
| **Forced belonging** | Requiring community participation | Make community opt-in and genuinely valuable |
| **Gatekeeping** | Arbitrary barriers to entry | Clear, fair criteria for exclusive communities |
| **Identity shaming** | Making non-members feel inferior | Invite, don't shame |
| **Performative unity** | "We" language without real community | Build genuine community before using unity language |
| **Cultural appropriation** | Borrowing identity markers from other communities | Build authentic identity from your own community's experience |

## Unity Design Checklist

- [ ] Have we named our community with an identity label (not just "users")?
- [ ] Are we using "we" language consistently in product copy?
- [ ] Do we have community rituals (regular events, shared activities)?
- [ ] Are there visible symbols of membership (badges, swag, visual markers)?
- [ ] Is co-creation a core part of the product experience?
- [ ] Do we publicly acknowledge and celebrate community contributions?
- [ ] Is our community built on positive identity (not just opposition to others)?
- [ ] Do onboarding flows make new users feel like they're joining a tribe?
- [ ] Are we creating opportunities for members to bond with each other (not just with us)?
- [ ] Does our community have a clear shared worldview or mission?

## Key Takeaways

1. Unity is not liking with extra steps; it is fundamentally about shared identity ("one of us")
2. The strongest unity sources are shared struggle, shared values, and co-creation
3. Language matters enormously: "we" includes, "you" distances
4. Naming the tribe is the first and most important step in building unity
5. Co-creation turns users into stakeholders with emotional ownership
6. Rituals, symbols, and inside language are the infrastructure of tribal identity
7. Unity must be positive and inclusive; toxic tribalism destroys communities from within
````

````markdown
---
name: influence-psychology
description: 'Apply the seven principles of ethical persuasion (reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity, unity) to product design, copy, and sales. Use when the user mentions "social proof", "persuasive copy", "why users dont convert", "ethical persuasion", "reciprocity", "scarcity tactics", "commitment and consistency", "shared identity", "in-group", "make my copy more persuasive", "increase trust", or "get more people to say yes". Also trigger when designing testimonial sections, crafting urgency messaging, or improving trust signals on landing pages. Covers the principles, when each applies, and ethical limits. For deal negotiation tactics, see negotiation. For viral word-of-mouth, see contagious.'
license: MIT
metadata:
  author: wondelai
  version: "1.4.1"
---

# Influence Psychology Framework

Apply six decades of persuasion science — Cialdini's research into why people say "yes" — to product, copy, and sales, ethically.

## Core Principle

**People don't make decisions rationally — they use mental shortcuts (heuristics) that can be triggered to influence behavior.** These shortcuts evolved because they're usually reliable, but they can also be exploited. Understanding them lets you design products, messaging, and experiences that align with how people actually decide.

## Scoring

**Goal: 10/10.** When reviewing or creating persuasive elements (features, copy, flows, campaigns), run the Quick Diagnostic, then score against the bands below and apply the ethics gate. Always report the current score and the specific change needed to reach 10/10.

- **9-10** — Multiple principles deliberately layered; every claim truthful; users can reverse the decision; passes the transparency test (still works if the user knows the strategy); safe for vulnerable users.
- **7-8** — Principles deliberately layered and honest, but one gap (e.g. weak reversibility, or a single principle where layering was possible).
- **5-6** — One principle present but generic, or leverage left on the table.
- **<=3** — No principle deliberately designed (relying on luck), OR any tactic is deceptive/coercive. Any fabricated proof, fake scarcity, or hidden-cost dark pattern caps the score at 3 regardless of other strengths.

## The Seven Principles of Influence

### 1. Reciprocity

**Core concept:** People feel obligated to give back to those who have given to them first.

**Why it works:** Humans are wired to avoid being indebted — the obligation to repay can overpower personal preference, and the return favor often exceeds the original gift.

**Key insights:**
- The gift must come first (before the request)
- Unexpected, personalized gifts beat expected, generic ones
- Even small gifts create obligation

**Product applications:**

| Context | Reciprocity Trigger | Example |
|---------|---------------------|---------|
| **Free trials** | Full access first, then ask to pay | Spotify Premium trial → subscription |
| **Content marketing** | Value upfront (guides, tools) | HubSpot free CRM → paid tools |
| **Referral programs** | Reward both referrer and referee | Dropbox: both get extra storage |

**Copy patterns:**
- "Here's a gift for you..." (before asking)
- "As a thank you for signing up..."
- "We noticed you needed help with X, so we..."

See [references/reciprocity.md](references/reciprocity.md) when building free trials, lead magnets, or referral rewards — gift tiers, email templates, day-by-day reciprocity-stacking, and A/B variables.

### 2. Commitment & Consistency

**Core concept:** People want to be consistent with their past statements, beliefs, and actions.

**Why it works:** Inconsistency is psychologically uncomfortable; once we take a stand, personal and interpersonal pressure pushes us to behave consistently with it.

**Key insights:**
- Small initial commitments lead to larger ones (foot-in-the-door)
- Public > private; written > verbal; active (user-generated) > passive
- Self-perception: we infer our attitudes from our behavior

**Product applications:**

| Context | Commitment Trigger | Example |
|---------|-------------------|---------|
| **Onboarding** | Easy yes, then larger asks | Duolingo: "Can you commit to 5 min/day?" |
| **Goal setting** | User publicly states a goal | Strava: "I want to run 50km this month" |
| **Habit formation** | Track streaks publicly | Snapchat streaks, GitHub contributions |

**Copy patterns:**
- "What's your biggest challenge with X?" (commitment to a problem)
- "How much would you like to save per month?" (numerical commitment)
- "You said you wanted to achieve X. Let's start with..."

**Onboarding sequence:** micro-commitment ("What brings you here?") → small action (click, choice) → public/written commitment (goal) → reinforce ("Based on what you told us...").

**Ethical boundary:** Make every commitment freely chosen and easily reversible — no trick opt-ins or locked-in defaults the user can't undo.

See [references/commitment-consistency.md](references/commitment-consistency.md) when designing onboarding or goal-setting flows — foot-in-the-door sequences and public-commitment tactics.

### 3. Social Proof

**Core concept:** People determine what's correct by finding out what others think is correct.

**Why it works:** When uncertain, we use others' behavior as a guide — "if everyone's doing it, it must be right."

**Key insights:**
- Most powerful when observers are uncertain; similar others = stronger proof
- Negative social proof backfires ("9 out of 10 don't...")
- Specific numbers beat vague claims ("2,347 users" > "thousands")

**Types of social proof:**

| Type | Definition | Example |
|------|------------|---------|
| **Wisdom of crowds** | Many people use/buy | "Join 50,000+ marketers" |
| **Wisdom of friends** | People you know use it | "3 of your friends use Notion" |
| **Expert** | Authorities endorse | "Recommended by Y Combinator" |
| **Celebrity** | Famous people use it | "Used by Elon Musk" |
| **Certification** | Third-party validation | "SOC 2 compliant", "App of the Year" |
| **User** | Similar people succeeded | "Startups like yours grew 10x" |

**Product applications:**

| Context | Social Proof Implementation | Example |
|---------|----------------------------|---------|
| **Landing pages** | User count, reviews, logos | "Trusted by 10,000+ companies" |
| **Signup flow** | Live signups, popular plans | "23 people signed up in the last hour" |
| **Feature adoption** | Show usage by others | "85% of teams use this feature" |

**Copy patterns:**
- "[X number] of [similar people] are already..."
- "[Name/Company] increased [metric] by [%]"
- "Don't take our word for it. Here's what [users] say..."

**Ethical boundary:** Disclose when proof is curated or cherry-picked (e.g. "selected reviews") rather than presenting it as representative.

See [references/social-proof.md](references/social-proof.md) when building testimonial sections or trust bars — proof types and implementation patterns.

### 4. Authority

**Core concept:** People follow the lead of credible, knowledgeable experts.

**Why it works:** Obedience to authority is deeply ingrained — following experts is an efficient shortcut when we lack expertise ourselves.

**Key insights:**
- Titles, credentials, even symbols (lab coats, official-looking design) trigger automatic compliance
- Admitting a weakness paradoxically increases authority (trustworthiness) — lead with it before strengths
- Expertise doesn't transfer across domains, but people assume it does

**Sources of authority:**

| Type | Signal | Example |
|------|--------|---------|
| **Credentials** | Degrees, certifications | "Built by Stanford PhDs" |
| **Experience** | Years in field, track record | "20 years in cybersecurity" |
| **Association** | Trusted partners, investors | "Backed by Y Combinator" |
| **Content** | Thought leadership, research | "Based on research with 10,000 users" |
| **Transparency** | Honest about limitations | "Works best for teams of 10-50" |

**Product applications:**

| Context | Authority Trigger | Example |
|---------|------------------|---------|
| **About page** | Founder and team expertise | "Built by ex-Google engineers" |
| **Content** | Original research, citations | "State of [Industry] 2026 Report" |
| **Partnerships** | Security certs, integration badges | "SOC 2 Type II", "GDPR compliant" |

**Copy patterns:**
- "Trusted by [authority figure/company]"
- "Research shows that [cite source]..."
- "Our team includes [credentials]"

See [references/authority.md](references/authority.md) when writing About pages, bylines, or trust badges — credential framing and thought-leadership strategies.

### 5. Liking

**Core concept:** People prefer to say yes to those they like.

**Why it works:** Each liking factor (similarity, compliments, cooperation) is a separate lever that independently lowers a person's resistance to a request — they stack.

**Factors that increase liking:**

| Factor | Mechanism | Example |
|--------|-----------|---------|
| **Attractiveness** | Halo effect: attractive = good | Professional headshots, polished design |
| **Similarity** | We like people like us | "I'm a founder just like you" |
| **Compliments** | Flattery works (even when obvious) | "You have great taste in tools" |
| **Cooperation** | Working toward shared goals | "Let's build this together" |
| **Familiarity** | Repeated exposure increases liking | Consistent brand, retargeting |
| **Association** | Linked to positive things | Placement with aspirational lifestyles |

**Product applications:**

| Context | Liking Trigger | Example |
|---------|---------------|---------|
| **Brand voice** | Friendly, conversational, human | Mailchimp's playful copy |
| **Team pages** | Real people, personality | Personal bios, hobbies, photos |
| **Support** | Warm, empathetic responses | "I totally understand that frustration..." |

**Copy patterns:**
- "We're [similar trait] just like you"
- "We built this because we were frustrated with..."
- Casual, warm language ("Hey", "Awesome!", "We got you")

See [references/liking.md](references/liking.md) when setting brand voice or writing support replies — liking factors and tone guidelines. For ready-to-adapt persuasive copy across all seven principles, see [references/copywriting.md](references/copywriting.md).

### 6. Scarcity

**Core concept:** People want more of what they can't have or what's running out.

**Why it works:** Loss aversion is stronger than gain seeking — FOMO triggers urgency, and psychological reactance makes us want what threatens to become unavailable.

**Key insights:**
- Scarcity of time > scarcity of quantity; newly scarce > always scarce (loss framing)
- Competition increases value — if others want it, I want it
- Exclusive access is more valuable than open access

**Types of scarcity:**

| Type | Mechanism | Example |
|------|-----------|---------|
| **Limited quantity** | Finite supply | "Only 5 seats left" |
| **Limited time** | Deadline pressure | "Offer ends Friday" |
| **Exclusive access** | Not everyone can have it | "Invite-only beta" |
| **Competition** | Others competing for it | "12 people viewing this" |

**Product applications:**

| Context | Scarcity Trigger | Example |
|---------|-----------------|---------|
| **Pricing** | Limited-time discount | "Early bird pricing ends in 3 days" |
| **Features** | Beta access, waitlist | "Join 5,000 on the waitlist" |
| **Inventory** | Stock levels | "2 left in stock" |

**Copy patterns:**
- "Limited to the first [X] customers"
- "Offer expires [specific date]"
- "[X] people are viewing this right now"

**Ethical boundary:** Ethical scarcity reflects real constraints (true inventory counts, genuine deadlines, legitimate capacity limits). Unethical: invented limits, countdown timers that reset, "Only 2 left!" shown daily, pressuring vulnerable users.

See [references/scarcity.md](references/scarcity.md) when adding urgency or waitlists — five scarcity types, each with an "ethical when" line and the dark patterns to avoid.

### 7. Unity

**Core concept:** People say yes to those they consider part of "us" (shared identity).

**Why it works:** Tribal identity is fundamental — we make sacrifices for in-group members we wouldn't make for strangers.

**Unity vs. Liking:** Liking = "this person is like me" (similarity); Unity = "this person is me" (shared identity).

**Sources of unity:**

| Type | Mechanism | Example |
|------|-----------|---------|
| **Place** | Hometown, region, nationality | "Built in San Francisco, for founders" |
| **Experience** | Shared hardship or triumph | "We've all struggled with bad CRMs" |
| **Values** | Deep beliefs, mission alignment | "For people who value privacy" |
| **Tribe** | Co-creation, movement | "Join the indie maker community" |

**Product applications:**

| Context | Unity Trigger | Example |
|---------|--------------|---------|
| **Brand positioning** | Define the tribe | "For remote-first teams" |
| **Messaging** | "We" language, shared struggle | "We believe work should be flexible" |
| **Community** | Facilitate co-creation | User-generated content, forums |

**Copy patterns:**
- "For [identity group]" ("For designers", "For bootstrappers")
- "Join [X] others who believe..."
- "We're building this together"

**Ethical boundary:** Build the in-group by what it stands for, not by vilifying an out-group — define "us" without manufacturing a "them" to resent.

See [references/unity.md](references/unity.md) when defining a brand tribe or community — identity-marketing and co-creation strategies.

## Combining Principles

The most powerful persuasion layers multiple principles:

**SaaS landing page:** authority ("Built by ex-Stripe engineers") + social proof ("Trusted by 5,000+ companies") + liking (warm copy) + scarcity ("Join the beta—limited spots") + reciprocity ("Start free, no credit card") + unity ("For founders who move fast").

**Referral program:** reciprocity (reward both parties) + social proof ("X friends already joined") + unity ("Invite your team") + commitment (ask after a good experience).

See [references/case-studies.md](references/case-studies.md) for full worked teardowns of multi-principle stacks across industries.

## The Ethical Line

**Persuasion helps people see value they'd appreciate anyway; manipulation tricks people into choices against their interests.** The deciding tests are in the Quick Diagnostic below — run every persuasive element through them before shipping.

See [references/ethics.md](references/ethics.md) when a tactic feels borderline or you ship to vulnerable users — the persuasion-vs-manipulation decision tree, the regulatory landscape (FTC, GDPR, DSA, dark-patterns law), vulnerable-population safeguards, and audit templates.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Why It Fails | Fix |
|---------|-------------|------|
| **Fake social proof** | Destroys trust when discovered | Use real data or don't use it |
| **Overuse of scarcity** | Becomes noise, loses power | Reserve for genuine urgency |
| **Inconsistent authority** | Undermines credibility | Don't claim expertise you lack |
| **Forced reciprocity** | Feels transactional, not genuine | Give without immediate ask |
| **Generic unity** | "Everyone" is not a tribe | Define specific shared identity |

## Quick Diagnostic

Audit any persuasive element:

| Question | If No | Action |
|----------|-------|--------|
| Which principle(s) am I using? | You're relying on luck | Explicitly design for influence |
| Am I combining principles? | Missing leverage | Layer multiple principles |
| Is this claim/tactic truthful? | You're manipulating | Remove or replace with truth |
| Does it help the user (not just convert)? | You're exploiting, not persuading | Realign the tactic with the user's goal |
| Would it still work if the user knew the strategy? | The tactic relies on deception | Replace with a transparent version |
| Can users easily reverse the decision? | Ethical concern | Add clear opt-outs |
| Safe for vulnerable users (children, elderly, distressed)? | Heightened-harm risk | Apply ethics.md safeguards or exclude them |

## Further Reading

Based on Robert Cialdini's research and books:

- [*"Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion"*](https://www.amazon.com/Influence-Psychology-Persuasion-Robert-Cialdini/dp/006124189X?tag=wondelai00-20) by Robert B. Cialdini (Original + Expanded Edition with Unity principle)
- [*"Pre-Suasion: A Revolutionary Way to Influence and Persuade"*](https://www.amazon.com/Pre-Suasion-Revolutionary-Way-Influence-Persuade/dp/1501109790?tag=wondelai00-20) by Robert B. Cialdini (Advanced: creating privileged moments for influence)

## About the Author

**Robert B. Cialdini, PhD** is Regents' Professor Emeritus of Psychology and Marketing at Arizona State University. *Influence*, the foundational text on persuasion science, has sold over 5 million copies worldwide, and he has consulted for Fortune 500 companies, government agencies, and nonprofits on ethical influence.
````

## File: plugins/sales-influence/skills/made-to-stick/references/applications.md
````markdown
# Applications: Applying SUCCESs Across Contexts

The SUCCESs framework is not theoretical — it is a practical toolkit that can be applied to any communication context. This reference provides step-by-step guidance for applying all six principles to landing pages, product demos, onboarding flows, presentations, email campaigns, internal communications, and documentation. Each section includes templates, checklists, and before/after examples.

## Applying SUCCESs to Landing Pages

A landing page has one job: convert a visitor into a lead or customer. Each SUCCESs principle strengthens a different part of that conversion process.

### Element-by-Element Breakdown

| Principle | Landing Page Element | Implementation |
|-----------|---------------------|----------------|
| **Simple** | Headline + subheadline | One value proposition. No compound sentences. No "and." |
| **Unexpected** | Above-the-fold hook | A counterintuitive claim or surprising statistic |
| **Concrete** | Benefits section | Specific outcomes with numbers, not abstract promises |
| **Credible** | Social proof section | Named customers, specific metrics, Sinatra Test logos |
| **Emotional** | Pain/aspiration section | One customer's story or a vivid problem description |
| **Stories** | Case study or testimonial | A complete character-problem-solution-outcome narrative |

### Landing Page Template

```
[HEADLINE: Simple — one core value proposition in under 10 words]
[SUBHEADLINE: Unexpected — counterintuitive claim or surprising angle]

[HERO SECTION]
- Concrete outcome #1 (specific number)
- Concrete outcome #2 (specific number)
- Concrete outcome #3 (specific number)
[CTA BUTTON]

[SOCIAL PROOF: Credible]
- Logo bar with named companies
- "Join [specific number] teams including [impressive name]"

[PAIN SECTION: Emotional]
- "You know the feeling when [specific, relatable pain]..."
- Individual focus: one person's experience

[STORY SECTION: Stories]
- Customer transformation narrative (character → problem → solution → outcome)
- Direct quote with name, title, and company

[CREDIBILITY SECTION: Credible]
- Specific metric: "[X] customers processed [Y] in the last month"
- Testable credential: "Try free for 14 days, no credit card"

[FINAL CTA]
```

### Before/After: Landing Page Headline

**Before:**
> "The All-in-One Platform for Modern Teams"
> "Streamline your workflow with AI-powered automation and seamless integrations."

**After:**
> "Ship 3x Faster Without Hiring"
> "Your competitor just launched in 2 weeks. Yours has been stuck for 2 months. Here is why."

## Applying SUCCESs to Product Demos

Product demos fail when they become feature tours. A sticky demo tells a story, creates curiosity, and delivers emotional impact.

### The Sticky Demo Framework

| Phase | Principle | What to Do |
|-------|-----------|-----------|
| **Opening (30 seconds)** | Unexpected + Emotional | Start with the customer's pain, not your product. State something surprising. |
| **Setup (1-2 minutes)** | Simple + Concrete | "Today I will show you ONE thing: how [specific outcome] happens in [specific time]" |
| **Demonstration (3-5 minutes)** | Concrete + Credible | Use real data, real names, real workflows. Time the action. |
| **Aha Moment (30 seconds)** | Unexpected | The moment where the old way vs. new way becomes viscerally clear |
| **Proof (1 minute)** | Credible + Stories | "Here is what [named customer] said after seeing this for the first time" |
| **Close (30 seconds)** | Emotional + Simple | Return to the pain. Show how it is now resolved. One CTA. |

### Demo Script Template

```
"Before I show you anything, let me ask you a question.
[UNEXPECTED: A question that reveals a pain they did not realize they had]

Here is what [REAL CUSTOMER NAME] was dealing with:
[EMOTIONAL: 2-sentence description of their specific problem]

Watch what happens when I [CONCRETE: specific action].
[DEMONSTRATE: real data, timed, specific]

See that? [SIMPLE: one sentence explaining what just happened]
That used to take [CREDIBLE: specific old time]. Now it takes [specific new time].

[CUSTOMER NAME] told us: '[STORY: direct quote about the impact].'

Want to try it with your own data? [CTA]"
```

### Before/After: Demo Opening

**Before:**
> "Hi, thanks for joining. Today I am going to give you a tour of our platform. Let me start with the dashboard..."

**After:**
> "Before I show you anything, I want you to think about the last time you needed a report for a meeting and could not find the right numbers in time. That happened to the VP of Sales at Notion last quarter. It cost them a $2M deal. Let me show you why that will never happen to you."

## Applying SUCCESs to Onboarding Flows

Onboarding is where most products lose users. A sticky onboarding flow guides users to their first "aha moment" as fast as possible while building belief and motivation.

### Screen-by-Screen Framework

| Screen | Principle | Content |
|--------|-----------|---------|
| **Welcome** | Unexpected + Emotional | Not "Welcome to [Product]." Instead: "In the next 3 minutes, you will see [specific surprising outcome]." |
| **Quick Win (Step 1)** | Simple + Concrete | One action. Show the result immediately. Use real data if possible. |
| **Progress** | Credible | "You are already ahead of 70% of new users who skip this step." |
| **Core Value (Step 2-3)** | Concrete + Unexpected | Deliver the "aha moment" — the thing that makes them say "Oh, THAT is what this does." |
| **Social Proof** | Credible + Stories | "[Name] at [Company] got to this point and never looked back. Here is what they built." |
| **Celebration** | Emotional | Celebrate the first success. Make them feel accomplished. |
| **Next Step** | Simple | One clear next action. Not a menu of 10 options. |

### Before/After: Onboarding Welcome Screen

**Before:**
> "Welcome to DataSync! Let us get you set up. Here are the 7 steps to get started."

**After:**
> "In 90 seconds, you will see all your customer data in one place for the first time. Ready? Let us start with one click: connect your CRM."

## Applying SUCCESs to Presentations and Pitches

Presentations fail when they are information dumps. A sticky presentation is structured as a journey with one core message, supported by surprise, proof, emotion, and story.

### The Sticky Presentation Structure

| Section | Duration | Principle | Content |
|---------|----------|-----------|---------|
| **Hook** | 30 seconds | Unexpected | Open with a surprising fact, a bold claim, or a mystery |
| **Problem** | 2-3 minutes | Emotional + Concrete | Make the audience feel the problem. Use one person's story. |
| **Core Insight** | 1 minute | Simple | State your one key message. This is your Commander's Intent. |
| **Evidence** | 5-7 minutes | Credible + Concrete | Prove your claim with specific data, demonstrations, and examples |
| **Story** | 2-3 minutes | Stories | A complete narrative that embodies your core message |
| **Implications** | 2 minutes | Unexpected + Emotional | "Here is what this means for you, specifically" |
| **CTA** | 30 seconds | Simple | One clear ask. Not three options. One. |

### Presentation Checklist

- [ ] The first slide has no logo, no agenda, no "About Us" — just the hook
- [ ] There is ONE core message (say it in 10 words or fewer)
- [ ] At least one moment will make the audience say "I did not know that"
- [ ] Every statistic is human-scale and compared to something familiar
- [ ] At least one real person's story is told with name, context, and outcome
- [ ] The audience knows exactly what to do next when it ends
- [ ] There are fewer than 20 slides for a 30-minute presentation
- [ ] No slide has more than 15 words on it

### Before/After: Presentation Opening Slide

**Before:**
> Slide 1: Company logo, "Q3 Strategic Review," date, presenter name, agenda

**After:**
> Slide 1: "47% of our customers almost left last quarter. Here is why they stayed."

## Applying SUCCESs to Email Campaigns

Email is the most competitive attention environment. Your message competes with 100+ other emails in a single inbox. SUCCESs principles help you win the open and the click.

### Email Framework

| Email Element | Principle | Implementation |
|--------------|-----------|----------------|
| **Subject line** | Unexpected + Simple | Pattern-breaking curiosity gap in under 8 words |
| **First sentence** | Concrete + Emotional | A specific, vivid pain or aspiration they can picture |
| **Body** | Stories + Credible | One story or proof point — not a catalog of features |
| **CTA** | Simple | One action. Not "Learn more, sign up, or reply." Just one. |

### Email Templates

**The Curiosity Gap Email:**
```
Subject: The mistake your team is making every Monday

[Name], last Monday your team probably spent 2 hours in a meeting
that could have been a 5-minute async update.

I know this because 84% of teams we surveyed do the same thing.

[Customer name] at [Company] eliminated Monday meetings entirely.
Their team shipped 30% more that quarter.

Here is the 2-minute change they made: [LINK]
```

**The Story Email:**
```
Subject: How [Name] saved 12 hours a week

Quick story:

[Name] runs ops at [Company]. Every Friday, she spent 3 hours
compiling a report nobody read.

One day she asked: "What if the report wrote itself?"

She found [Product]. Setup took 15 minutes. The next Friday,
the report was in her inbox at 8am. She went to a yoga class instead.

Want your Fridays back? [CTA]
```

**The Surprising Stat Email:**
```
Subject: You are losing $4,200/month (here is the math)

[Name], your team has 12 people. Each one spends ~30 minutes/day
on [specific manual task].

That is 130 hours/month. At your team's average hourly cost,
that is $4,200 going to a task a machine can do.

Here is the math: [LINK]
And here is the fix: [CTA]
```

## Applying SUCCESs to Internal Communications

Internal communications are where the Curse of Knowledge does the most damage. Everyone assumes shared context. Nobody questions the jargon. Ideas die in the noise of Slack and email.

### Making Internal Messages Stick

| Principle | Internal Application | Example |
|-----------|---------------------|---------|
| **Simple** | One message per communication. No "3 things" emails. | "This quarter's priority: reduce churn. Everything else supports that." |
| **Unexpected** | Lead with the surprising data point | "We lost more customers last month than in the previous 6 months combined." |
| **Concrete** | Use real examples from the team's experience | "Remember the Acme Corp escalation last Tuesday? That is the exact problem we are solving." |
| **Credible** | Share the data behind the decision | "Here are the 47 customer interviews that led to this conclusion." |
| **Emotional** | Make the impact personal | "If we do not fix this, the support team will keep working weekends." |
| **Stories** | Tell the story of a real customer or team member | "Let me tell you what happened when our newest engineer tried to deploy for the first time." |

### Before/After: Company All-Hands Announcement

**Before:**
> "We are excited to announce a strategic realignment of our go-to-market motion. Effective next quarter, we will be transitioning to a product-led growth model with enhanced self-serve capabilities and optimized conversion funnels."

**After:**
> "Starting next quarter, customers can buy our product without ever talking to a salesperson. Why? Because 60% of our signups already try to buy online and give up. We are losing $200K/month to a 'Contact Sales' button. Here is what changes."

## Applying SUCCESs to Documentation and Help Content

Documentation is the most undervalued communication channel. Great documentation reduces support tickets, improves onboarding, and builds trust. But most documentation is cursed by knowledge.

### The Sticky Documentation Framework

| Principle | Documentation Application |
|-----------|--------------------------|
| **Simple** | One concept per page. Clear hierarchy. Lead with the answer, not the context. |
| **Unexpected** | Call out common mistakes upfront. "Most users try X first. Here is why Y works better." |
| **Concrete** | Every instruction includes a screenshot or code example. Never say "configure as needed." |
| **Credible** | Include "Why" sections explaining the reasoning. Link to source documentation. |
| **Emotional** | Acknowledge the user's frustration. "We know this is confusing. Here is the simplest path." |
| **Stories** | Include use case examples. "Here is how a marketing team uses this feature to..." |

### Before/After: Help Article

**Before:**
> **Setting Up Integrations**
> Navigate to the Settings panel and select the Integrations tab. Configure your desired integrations by providing the necessary credentials and selecting the appropriate sync options.

**After:**
> **Connect Slack in 60 Seconds**
> Want your team to get notified in Slack when a deal closes? Here is how:
> 1. Click Settings (gear icon, top right)
> 2. Click Integrations
> 3. Find Slack and click Connect
> 4. Choose your channel (most teams pick #sales-wins)
> 5. Done. Your next closed deal will trigger a celebration message.
>
> Common mistake: Choosing #general instead of a specific channel. Your team will tune it out within a week.

## Master Checklist: SUCCESs Audit for Any Context

Before publishing any communication, verify each principle:

- [ ] **Simple:** ONE core message, understandable by a 12-year-old, most important info first
- [ ] **Unexpected:** Opens with a pattern-break, creates a curiosity gap, surprise serves the core message
- [ ] **Concrete:** Abstractions replaced with examples, numbers are human-scale, audience can picture it
- [ ] **Credible:** Proof point included, testimonials use real names, claims are verifiable or testable
- [ ] **Emotional:** Connects to a feeling, features an individual's experience, answers "What is in it for me?"
- [ ] **Stories:** Includes a narrative with character + problem + resolution, illustrates the core message

## Quick Reference: One-Line SUCCESs Reminders

| Principle | One-Line Reminder |
|-----------|-------------------|
| **Simple** | "If they remember one thing, what must it be?" |
| **Unexpected** | "What will make them look up from their phone?" |
| **Concrete** | "Can they picture it happening?" |
| **Credible** | "Why should they believe me?" |
| **Emotional** | "What will they feel?" |
| **Stories** | "Whose story illustrates this?" |
````
